name: project_multi_credential_types_plan
description: "Post-6.0 plan (drafted 2026-09-16): support every credential type a lock can hold, starting with password; Raman's six requirements, verified facts, and the open design questions"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: fadb7389-15f9-469d-b9a2-4d12e0c7cead
  modified: 2026-09-16T19:03:50.052Z
---

Raman's direction on 2026-09-16, to ship after 6.0 (6.0 released that day), and after [[project_unanswered_reads_degrade]], which Raman wants done first. The model must fit every credential type; the first new one is **password**, because it needs no reader hardware. Supersedes the open questions in [[project_password_credential_expansion]]; builds on [[per-credential-type-in-sync-sensors]].

## Requirements (Raman's words, condensed)

1. An entry's **available credential types** are the union of the types its locks support (3 locks with PIN, 2 also with NFC → PIN and NFC).
2. Setting or clearing a credential of a type writes **only the entry's locks that support that type**.
3. Every type gets its own in-sync sensor: the same class that serves `pin_in_sync` (one class, the key differs).
4. "A user requires a PIN" becomes "a user requires **at least one** supported credential". Every type accepts an empty value; a user with none is disabled.
5. Card: where the PIN input is today, tabs or icons per type, selecting one shows that input. Raman is open to other ways to show several credentials for one user.
6. Card: only the entry's available types are selectable.

## Verified facts (2026-09-16, main after 6.0)

- `CredentialType` already has PIN, RFID, FINGERPRINT, FACE, PASSWORD, NFC. `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` (domain/credentials.py) is the single switch, PIN only.
- `CredentialTypeCapability` has `num_slots`, `min_length`, `max_length`, `supports_learn`.
- Providers today: **Z-Wave** reads PIN, password, RFID, NFC, face, fingerprint (`zwave_js.py` type map) but `async_get_capabilities` reports **only PIN**. **Matter** reports only PIN; HA's `matter.lock_helpers` supports PIN, RFID, fingerprint, face (no password, no NFC) and exposes `max_rfid_users`/`min_rfid_length`/`max_rfid_length`. **Virtual** advertises every type. ZHA, Zigbee2MQTT, Schlage, Akuvox, zwave-js-ui MQTT: PIN only (base default).
- So password is **Z-Wave User Credential CC only** (plus Virtual) among real providers.
- Already type-generic: sync managers keyed by `CredentialAddress(user_ref, type)`, one per type, owned by `SlotEntityCoordinator`; in-sync sensor class parameterized by addresses, `credential_in_sync_key(type)`; `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` (const.py + ts/const.ts, contract-tested); `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS`; `set_credential`/`clear_credential` take `credential_type` (refuse non-PIN today); `credential_used` event reports the credential kind.
- Still PIN-shaped: `_VALUE_ENTITY_KEYS` in sync.py (PIN → `pin` text entity only), the `pin_required` repair and enable guard in slot_coordinator.py, subentry/setup/YAML field `pin`, `generate_pin`, card PIN input, `mask_pin` in logs, capability checks at lock setup ("does not advertise PIN").
- Known gap from the #1572 review: `managed_addresses(slot)` is global, so today a second managed type would give every lock a manager for it and turn the aggregate `in_sync` unavailable on locks without that type. Requirement 2 fixes this by filtering per lock.

## How types differ when set (answered for Raman 2026-09-16)

Value types share one call shape (type, index, value); what differs is the value and the lock's limits. PIN is ASCII digits; password is free text within the lock's length bounds; Matter takes RFID as a hex string it converts to bytes. Each type has its own slot count and length bounds per lock. HA's `zwave_js.lock_helpers.async_set_credential` documents PIN/password only; `matter.lock_helpers` validates PIN and RFID. Biometrics (fingerprint, face) have no value: they are enrolled at the lock (Z-Wave `supports_learn`; Matter cannot enroll remotely).

## Decisions (Raman, 2026-09-16)

- **Scope:** value types only in the first release: PIN, password, RFID, NFC. The model stays ready for biometrics; no biometric UI yet.
- **Index per type:** each credential type gets its **own index on the lock**, chosen when that credential is first set, independent of the user's slot number. A user on slot 20 can hold a password on a lock with 5 password slots. Needs per-(user, lock, type) index bookkeeping; the slot number stays the user's identity. (Today `credential_index_follows_slot` pins Z-Wave's PIN index to the slot; Matter already auto-allocates. Decide whether PIN keeps following the slot for back-compat -- likely yes.)
- **Per-type in-sync sensors:** one per type **that lock supports**, **always disabled by default**. The aggregate `in_sync` is what most people watch.
- **Card:** explore **tabs or icon chips** per available type over one input (a dot marking the ones set), expecting we may fall back to **one row per type**. Only the entry's available types are selectable.
- **A type no longer available** (its last capable lock removed): **keep the stored value, hide it** (remove its entity); it comes back if a capable lock is added again.
- **No matching credential on a lock** (user has only a password, lock is PIN-only): that lock holds **nothing** for them, and their aggregate `in_sync` there is **on** when it indeed holds nothing.
- **Generator:** generalize `generate_pin` so it also makes **passwords** within the lock's length limits. No generator for RFID/NFC (their values come from a tag).
- **Duplicates:** **refuse** a value another user in the entry already has **for the same type**; the same value across different types is fine.

## Derived plan (proposal, not yet confirmed)

- Available types per entry = union over the entry's locks of `capabilities.credential_types` ∩ `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`; managed addresses per lock = the user's types ∩ that lock's types (fixes the global `managed_addresses` gap). Recompute on lock add/remove and capability refresh.
- Providers: Z-Wave reports password/RFID/NFC capabilities; Matter reports RFID (PIN already); slot-only providers stay PIN.
- Config: user subentry and setup YAML gain `password`, `rfid`, `nfc` next to `pin`, all optional; `add_user`, `set_credential`, `clear_credential` accept them (the last two already take `credential_type`).
- Entities: a value text entity per available type (password in password mode), created and removed as availability changes; `_VALUE_ENTITY_KEYS` in sync.py maps each type to its key.
- Enable rule: `pin_required` becomes a credential-required rule and repair (at least one credential of an available type); clearing the last credential disables the user.
- Validation per type from capabilities: digits for PIN, length bounds for all, hex for RFID (and NFC, to confirm).
- Logs and diagnostics: generalize `mask_pin` masking to every credential value; `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS` already follows `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`.
- Phasing: password first (Z-Wave User Credential CC and Virtual are the only providers that hold it), then RFID/NFC (Matter RFID, Z-Wave RFID/NFC). Likely a 6.x minor release, since the changes are additive -- confirm with Raman.

PR #1227's `_project_users_to_slots` refactor wires "Option A" — the base class is now the per-credential-type chokepoint, so adding a second supported type does not touch providers. The next supported type is expected to be **password**, because the Z-Wave User Credential Command Class already exposes it natively.

**What's in place (after PR #1227):**
- Providers store every credential type they can map to the domain `CredentialType` enum. Z-Wave maps PIN_CODE, PASSWORD, RFID_CODE, NFC, FACE_BIOMETRIC, FINGER_BIOMETRIC; non-domain types (BLE, UWB, DESFIRE, unspecified/eye/hand biometric) are dropped.
- `BaseLock._project_users_to_slots(credential_type)` returns a `dict[int, SlotCredential]` for any credential type.
- `async_get_usercodes()` is now a thin PIN-shaped wrapper over that helper. `User.credentials_of_type(type)` is the generic accessor; `pin_credentials` delegates to it.
- TODO(option-b) annotation lives on `_project_users_to_slots` in `_base.py`.

**What's still open — "Option B" (entity-type scoping):**
The question is whether the coordinator/entities should stay slot-keyed-and-PIN-implicit or become type-scoped from the top — one set of slot entities per credential type. Pushing through a parametric projection is fine for one extra type; it gets awkward when the user needs separate slot ranges, automations, dashboards per type.

**Open UX/config questions to resolve before shipping password support:**
- Do users configure "PIN slots 1-10" and "password slots 1-5" as separate config blocks, or is each slot polymorphic (you pick the type per slot)?
- Are slot numbers shared across credential types on the lock side? Z-Wave indexes are per-(user_id, type, slot), so slot 1 PIN and slot 1 password can coexist — that argues for type-scoped slot ranges in the config.
- Do passwords get their own slot entity tree, or do existing entities gain a type attribute?
- Matter modeling: DoorLock cluster also has credential types, but Matter integration support is currently PIN-only — does password support need to wait on the Matter side, or does Z-Wave-only password support make sense as a first step?

**How to apply:** Don't pre-build entity-type scoping when adding password support — start by exercising the existing `_project_users_to_slots` chokepoint with PASSWORD and see how far that gets before the polymorphic-slot question forces a decision. The architecture is designed to let Option B happen when it earns its complexity.

**Superseded 2026-09-16** by [[project_multi_credential_types_plan]], which records Raman's answers to the open questions above.

# User-Centric Credential Model

**Date:** 2026-08-16
**Status:** Approved

## Goal

Lift Lock Code Manager's organizing unit from the *slot* to the *user*, and
support more than one credential type per user.

The provider layer already reached this shape in the PR 1–7 credential
management refactor: `domain/credentials.py` defines `User`, `Credential`,
`CredentialRef`, and `LockCapabilities`, and `BaseLock` orchestrates
user-first (`async_set_user` then `async_set_credential`). Providers already
store every credential type they can map — `zwave_js.py` maps Personal
Identification Number, password, Radio Frequency Identification, Near Field
Communication, face, and fingerprint today.

Everything *above* the provider seam is still slot-based:
`LockUsercodeUpdateCoordinator` is `dict[int, SlotCredential]`,
`EntryConfig.slots` is slot-keyed, entity and device identifiers are
slot-keyed, and `BaseLock._project_users_to_slots(CredentialType.PIN)` is the
funnel that discards every other type.

This work is therefore **not** "adopt a user model". It is **lift the existing
seam from the provider boundary to the entity boundary**.

## Non-goals

- Learn-at-device credential types (fingerprint, face). They have no value
  Lock Code Manager can author, so the convergence predicate that the entire
  sync engine is built on has no fixed point to reach. Deferred; see
  "Deferred work".
- Any change to the on-lock write primitives. The provider layer is done.
- Multiple users of differing user types, schedules, or duress credentials.
on startup, and raise a repair issue when the pairing is ambiguous.

### Entities exist only for configured types

A user gets entities for the credential types explicitly added to them. A
Personal Identification Number only user has exactly today's entity count.

The alternative — creating entities for every type the lock advertises via
`LockCapabilities.credential_types` — quadruples every user's entity count
on a lock advertising four types, most of them permanently blank.

This matters because entity count multiplies. Today it is `U*5 + U*L*2`;
under the new topology it is `U*4 + U*T*1 + U*T*L*2`. Ten users across two
locks: 90 entities today, 140 with two credential types, 190 with three.
Home Assistant handles that, but the config flow and the dashboard card do
not want to render a 19-entity user detail view.

### One event entity per user

`event.pin_used` becomes `event.credential_used`, fires at the user level
for any credential, and carries `credential_type` in the event data

Four sub-projects, each with its own spec, plan, and implementation cycle.
Only one is breaking.

| # | Sub-project | Release | User-visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | `CredentialAddress` seam: coordinator accessors and sync addressed by `(user_ref, CredentialType)`; storage untouched | minor | **None** |
| **B** | Coordinator storage flip, config schema v4, user-centric config flow, entity topology, entity re-slug and repair, websocket, diagnostics, dashboard card, blueprints | **v3.0.0** | Everything |
| **C** | Second credential type end to end (password on Z-Wave User Credential Command Class) | minor | Additive |
| **D** | Device-index auto-allocation on tag-capable locks; more than one credential per type per user | minor | Additive |

**Why A ships first and alone.** It is a pure internal re-key with no
user-visible surface, so it can ship and soak independently. It is also
where the risk concentrates: every convergence bug this integration has had
lived in the sync path. Under a "no behavior change" contract, the full test
suite and the Hypothesis properties act as a genuine oracle — any behavioral
difference is a bug, not an intended change. Folded into B, a failing test
would mean debugging a re-key and a schema migration simultaneously.

In sub-project A `user_ref` is still the slot number and the credential type
is always Personal Identification Number, so every coordinator key is
`(n, PIN)` and behavior is provably identical. The schema is untouched —
A ships against the existing slot-keyed configuration.

**Why B is one release rather than three.** The schema migration, the entity
re-slug, and the card and websocket changes are mutually dependent. The card
cannot render entities that have not been re-slugged, and the config flow
cannot edit a schema that has not been migrated. Splitting them ships
intermediate states that are individually broken.

**Why C precedes D.** C exercises the second-type path while every
credential is still pinned to its leased index, so a failure is
unambiguously a type-plumbing bug. D then removes the pinning with the
multi-type path already proven.

## Deferred work

- **Learn-at-device credential types.** `CredentialTypeCapability` already
  carries `supports_learn`. Fingerprint and face need an enrollment state
  machine (trigger learn mode, observe the device, represent "waiting for
  finger", handle timeout and abort) that sits alongside the convergence
  model rather than reusing it. Revisit after D.
- **Per-user schedules and user types.** `UserType` and `CredentialRule` are
  modeled minimally with a single member each precisely so this is additive.

## Open questions for implementation

It covers:

• `event.credential_used` replaces `pin_used` and carries `credential_type`.

In `2026-10-14-milestone-5.md`, "fingerprint" means the BLAKE2b hash of what was written, not the credential type. ### The more complete record is in memory, not docs - **`project_multi_credential_types_plan.md`** (2026-09-16) is the closest thing to a real spec. It has your six requirements, the facts I checked against the code then (which providers report which types), and your decisions: - First release covers value types only: PIN, password, RFID, NFC. - Each type gets its own index on the lock. - Per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default. - A user needs at least one credential, not specifically a PIN. - Duplicate values are refused within a type and allowed across types. - `generate_pin` is generalized to make passwords. - The card shows tabs or chips, one per type. Base directory for this skill: /Users/raman/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/5.0.7/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

class LockCodeManagerText(BaseLockCodeManagerEntity, TextEntity):
    """Text entity for lock code manager."""

    # Defaults for keys with no length constraint (the slot name) and the
    # fallback when bound locks advertise nothing or an unsatisfiable range.
    _DEFAULT_MIN = 0
    _DEFAULT_MAX = 9999

    def __init__(
        self,
        hass: HomeAssistant,
        ent_reg: er.EntityRegistry,
        config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
        slot_num: int,
        key: str,
        text_mode: TextMode,

        The advertised per-lock minimum is deliberately NOT surfaced here.
        Home Assistant's ``text.set_value`` service rejects
        ``len(value) < native_min`` before the value reaches the coordinator,
        which would block the empty string that clears a slot and would replace
        the coordinator's per-lock error with a generic one. The coordinator
        (``SlotEntityCoordinator._validate_credential_length``) is the
        authoritative minimum gate; an empty PIN is exempt because it clears
        the slot.
        """
        return self._DEFAULT_MIN

    @property
    @override
    def native_max(self) -> int:
        """
        Return the maximum value length -- always the permissive default.

        The advertised maximum is deliberately NOT surfaced here, for the same
        reason as the minimum. Home Assistant turns ``native_max`` into the
        field's ``maxlength``, so a lock advertising a limit lower than it
        really accepts would stop the keystrokes with no message at all: the
        field simply refuses to grow and nothing says why. The coordinator
        refuses the write instead, naming the lock and the range it claims,
        which is what somebody needs to see to recognise a bad advertisement.
        """
        return self._DEFAULT_MAX

    @property
    @override
    def native_value(self) -> str | None:
        """Return native value."""

class CredentialType(StrEnum):
    """
    Kind of credential a user presents to a lock.

    Lock Code Manager writes only ``PIN`` (``MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES``), but
    a use is reported as whichever kind the lock says was presented: ``PIN``,
    ``RFID`` or ``FINGERPRINT`` (Matter, ZHA, Zigbee2MQTT) or ``FACE``
    (Matter). ``PASSWORD`` and ``NFC`` are reserved so a future expansion to
    more kinds is additive. The members map cleanly to both the Z-Wave User
    Credential Command Class and the Matter DoorLock cluster credential-type
    vocabularies. ``PIN`` deliberately serializes to the lowercase wire value
    the providers already send.
    """

    PIN = "pin"
    RFID = "rfid"  # Radio Frequency Identification tag/card.
    FINGERPRINT = "fingerprint"
    FACE = "face"
    PASSWORD = "REDACTED"
    NFC = "nfc"  # Near Field Communication tag.

# write to a lock. Only PIN today, because a slot holds one PIN per user, and
# that is the only credential this integration knows how to produce.
#

# set anywhere else: the point of naming it is that "PIN is the only one" is a
# fact about today rather than an invariant, and every site that assumes it
# has to move together.
#
# Distinct from what a lock can REPORT. A lock may advertise types Lock Code
# Manager cannot write -- an RFID reader on the door is one -- and a use of
# one of those is still a use worth recording.
MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES: frozenset[CredentialType] = frozenset({CredentialType.PIN})


class UserType(StrEnum):

    *device* using the identifiers the lock allocated. ``CredentialAddress``
    is the integration-side handle the coordinator and the sync engine key
    on: which managed user, and which kind of credential.

    because the slot number is still the only user handle the configuration
    has. Once the configuration migrates to named users it becomes the
    user's name. Keeping both stages behind this one alias is what makes
    that a one-place type change rather than a second re-key.
    """

    credential_type: CredentialType


def managed_addresses(user_ref: int) -> tuple[CredentialAddress, ...]:
    """Return every credential address Lock Code Manager keeps in sync for a user."""
    return tuple(
        CredentialAddress(user_ref, credential_type)
        for credential_type in sorted(MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES)
    )


def pin_address(user_ref: int) -> CredentialAddress:
    """
    Build the Personal Identification Number address for a managed user.

    Every address in the integration is a PIN address today. This exists so
    the call sites that assume that say so explicitly, and so adding a
    second credential type surfaces each one as a place that needs a
    decision rather than silently continuing to mean PIN.
    """
    return CredentialAddress(user_ref, CredentialType.PIN)

    type fields already exist. ``credentials`` is mutable (a list), so this
    aggregate is intentionally not frozen; the contained ``Credential``
    values are themselves immutable.

        users into a slot-shaped view for a given credential kind. Providers
        store every type they can map (see each provider's ``async_get_users``);

        second supported type (Z-Wave User Credential CC also exposes

            for credential in self.credentials

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CredentialTypeCapability:
    """
    Per-credential-type limits advertised by a lock.

    ``num_slots`` is the number of slots the lock exposes for this credential
    type, ``min_length`` / ``max_length`` bound an acceptable value, and
    ``supports_learn`` is True when the lock can enroll the credential at the
    device (for example a fingerprint learn flow) rather than being told the
    value.

    Length convention shared by every provider: a non-positive ``max_length``
    means "no advertised maximum / unknown" -- never a literal zero-length
    limit, which would be meaningless -- so providers map an absent or
    unreadable maximum to ``0`` (Matter's ``max_pin_length or 0`` idiom). A
    non-positive ``min_length`` means "no minimum". ``length_bounds`` applies
    this normalization; do not emit a literal ``0`` to express a real limit.
    """

    num_slots: int
    min_length: int
    max_length: int
    supports_learn: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class LockCapabilities:
    """
    What a lock can do, as a platform-neutral snapshot.

    ``supports_user_management`` mirrors the providers' existing gate;
    ``max_users`` is the total number of users the lock can hold; and
    ``credential_types`` maps each supported ``CredentialType`` to its
    per-type limits. A type absent from the mapping is unsupported.
    """

    supports_user_management: bool
    max_users: int
    credential_types: Mapping[CredentialType, CredentialTypeCapability]
    # Maximum user-name length the lock will store; 0 means the lock has
    # no concept of named users (e.g. Z-Wave User Code CC) and the user
    # IS the credential. The base orchestration skips the separate user
    # write when ``supports_user_management`` is False OR this is 0.
    max_user_name_length: int = 0

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:

        object.__setattr__(
            self,
            "credential_types",
            MappingProxyType(dict(self.credential_types)),

        internally (zwave-js 15.24.3+ defers to User Code CC when User

        universal read projection (``_pin_state`` maps a withheld code to

"""
One slot on one lock: what is wanted, what was written, what the lock said.

Pure: no Home Assistant, no asyncio; the worker passes the time in. The
rules are the credential-model decisions as the first-principles design
states them (docs: 2026-10-13-core-first-principles.md).
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum, StrEnum
import hashlib
from typing import override

# What the lock said about a slot.


class Seen(Enum):
    """What the lock said about a slot, apart from which PIN it holds."""

    EMPTY = "empty"
    # Holds a code it will not show.
    MASKED = "masked"
    # Holds a code that is not in force.
    DISABLED = "disabled"
    # Answered without saying anything about the slot.
    SILENT = "silent"


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Holds:
    """The slot holds this PIN, and the lock said so."""

    pin: str = field(repr=False)

    @override
    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        """Keep the PIN out of logs (#917)."""
        return "Holds(****)"


Reading = Seen | Holds

# A wanted PIN, or None for an empty slot.
Want = str | None


class Repair(StrEnum):
    """Why a slot is held, and what the user is told."""

    # The lock refused the PIN; the slot is turned off.
    SLOT_DISABLED = "slot_disabled"
    # The PIN would not go on; nothing is written until the target changes.
    CANT_SET = "cant_set"
    # A clear would not take: the code may still open the door.
    CODE_MAY_REMAIN = "code_may_remain"


class Status(StrEnum):
    """A slot's sync status, as the integration shows it."""

content.text:
I've read enough to start the design. A few findings shape the questions, and one of them answers part of what you asked.

### What `main` looks like now
- **The sync core handles PINs only.** `sync/slot.py`, `sync/worker.py` and `sync/registry.py` key everything by slot number, and `LockPort.write(slot, pin)` takes one PIN per slot. None of the three refers to a credential type at all. Most of the password work is therefore in the sync core, not in the entity. The entity class is the easy part.
- **Locks that can hold a password:** Z-Wave (User Credential CC) and Virtual. Matter's DoorLock cluster has no password type. ZHA, Z2M, Schlage and Akuvox handle PINs only. Today the Z-Wave provider reports only PIN capabilities (`providers/zwave_js.py:466`) even though it already maps the PASSWORD type when reading.
- **Side finding to check later:** for a User Code CC lock whose keypad accepts non-digit characters, the driver uses the *Password* type instead of PIN (`node-zwave-js AccessControl.ts:1598`). Such a lock may be invisible to LCM today.

### Can the entity enforce a regex and min/max length?
Mostly. Home Assistant's `TextEntity` has `pattern`, `native_min` and `native_max`, and checks them in **two** places: in `text.set_value`, and also **when it renders the state** (`text/__init__.py:162-178` raises `ValueError` if the stored value violates them). The PIN entity deliberately leaves length out of these (`text.py:73-104`) for three reasons:
1. Clearing a credential means setting `""`, which a `native_min` would reject.
2. One entity covers several locks with different limits. A static bound is wrong for some of them, and HA's error message can't say which lock objected.
3. `native_max` becomes the browser's `maxlength`, so typing just stops with no explanation.

My proposal follows the same split:
- **The entity** (a new password text class, separate as you suggested) carries only the rules that come from the credential type itself, as a `pattern` that also allows an empty value.
- **The coordinator** keeps checking length per lock, and its error names the lock.

That leaves one question: what characters a password may contain.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Because HA re-checks `pattern` at state render, a pattern is a hard constraint on *stored* values, not just new input. If a later release tightens it, a value already saved under the looser rule makes the entity fail to render. Choose the character set as if it can only ever get looser.
- On the wire, Z-Wave's credential length field counts bytes (`UserCredentialCC.ts:2716`), and the driver decodes passwords as UTF-8 (`:82`). One accented character is two bytes, so a Unicode password could fail a lock's length limit even though it looks short enough to the user.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The multi-type plan from 2026-09-16 already settled several things: each type gets its own index on the lock, available types are the union across the entry's locks, per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default, a user needs at least one credential, duplicates are refused within a type, and `generate_pin` is generalized to passwords. I'll keep all of those unless you say otherwise. When we get to the card, I'll render the tab/icon options as mockups so you can compare them visually.

options.label: Printable ASCII (Recommended)
options.description: Space through ~ (0x20–0x7E). One character = one byte, so lock length limits mean what users see; matches what keypads and apps can enter. Pattern: ^[\x20-\x7E]*$

options.label: Printable ASCII, no spaces
options.description: 0x21–0x7E. Avoids leading/trailing-space confusion in a masked field, at the cost of rejecting passphrases with spaces.

options.label: Any Unicode except control chars
options.description: Most permissive. Length checks must count UTF-8 bytes, not characters, and the error has to explain why 'café' is 5 long.

options.label: No pattern; the lock decides
options.description: Entity enforces nothing; a rejected write surfaces as the existing per-slot 'can't set' repair.

class LockPort(Protocol):
    """What the worker needs from a provider."""

    async def read(self, slots: Collection[int]) -> Mapping[int, Reading]:
        """
        Return what the lock says about each of ``slots`` now; raise ``LockError``.

        Never a cache: a write is checked by reading its slot back, and a
        cached old value would count against a write that worked (#873,
        #1090). A provider that cannot read the lock itself leaves the slot
        out, and the write is trusted. Cached views come in as pushes.
        """
        ...

    async def write(self, slot: int, pin: str | None) -> bool | None:
        """
        Put ``pin`` in ``slot``, or clear it for None; raise ``LockError``.

        False when the lock answered that there was nothing to change -- a
        clear that found nothing: that says nothing about what the slot holds.
        """
        ...


@dataclass
class LockWorker[P: LockPort]:
    """The one owner of a lock's slots and of every exchange with it."""

    port: P
    salt: bytes
    gap: float = 2.0
    # Seconds one exchange may take before it counts as no answer.
    budget: float = 60.0
    clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic
    sleep: Callable[[float], Awaitable[None]] = asyncio.sleep
    on_change: Callable[[], None] = lambda: None
    # A write is about to be sent: what was written before is no longer
    # known to be there, and whatever remembers it has to forget it now --
    # the write may land and Home Assistant stop before it returns.
    on_send: Callable[[], None] = lambda: None
    # The lock refused this slot's PIN: the integration turns the slot off and
    # owns the repair that says why.
    on_disable: Callable[[int], None] = lambda slot: None
    # What was last written to a slot before this worker, by an earlier run:
    # a slot starts from it, so a lock that will not show its codes is not
    # written again (#405).
    recall: Callable[[int], str | None] = lambda slot: None
    # The lock answered an earlier run: one not answering now is offline.
    answered_before: bool = False
    slots: dict[int, Slot] = field(default_factory=dict)
    # What the logs call the lock (its entity id).
    name: str = "lock"
    async def turn[T](self, call: Callable[[], Awaitable[T]]) -> T:
        """
        Run ``call`` against the lock in its turn, as one exchange; return its result.

        For a question about the lock asked through a provider of its own (the
        migration's unmanaged-code sweep): nothing else talks to the lock
        meanwhile, and its answer counts like any other.
        """
        if self._stopping:
            raise LockError(ErrorKind.NO_ANSWER, sent=False, message="stopped")
        done: asyncio.Future[T] = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
        self._put(_Job("turn", call=call, done=done), "caller")
        return await done

Printable ASCII it is. The pattern will be `^[\x20-\x7E]*$`, so one character is always one byte and the lock's length limits mean what the user sees.

### The bigger decision: how the sync core holds a second credential type
`LockWorker` describes itself as *"the one owner of a lock's slots and of every exchange with it"* (`sync/worker.py:136`). It holds the state that belongs to the lock as a whole: pacing (`_pace`), whether the lock is offline or has answered before, and `turn()`, which keeps everything else off the lock during an exchange. Everything inside it is keyed by `slot: int`. There are three ways to fit password in:

- **A. Key the worker by credential address: `(slot, type)` instead of `slot`** (recommended). There is still one worker per lock, so the "one owner" principle holds. A `Slot` keeps exactly one value, so `sync/slot.py` (`wrote`, `seen`, the repairs) barely changes. The cost is retyping the keys through `worker.py` (971 lines), `registry.py` and `adapter.py`, and widening `LockPort.read/write` to take an address. Each type gets its own status and repairs, which the per-type in-sync sensors need anyway.
- **B. One worker per (lock, type).** This barely touches the core. But it breaks the "one owner" principle: two workers would each pace the lock, track whether it's offline, and run their own `turn()`. That means competing radio traffic and two offline repairs for a single dead lock. It's the same kind of split ownership as #1562.
- **C. A slot holds a bundle of credentials: `want = {pin: …, password: …}`.** The keys stay as they are, but `wrote`, `seen` and the repairs all become per-type maps inside one slot. When the PIN lands and the password doesn't, one slot ends up half-synced. This puts the complexity into the part of the core that was rewritten specifically to be simple.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The first-principles rewrite made the `Slot` a pure state machine over *one* value. Option A keeps it that way: the unit of sync becomes "one credential of one type on one lock", and only the key that identifies it changes. That's why A costs more lines than B or C but adds far less risk.
- Per-type indexes (decided 2026-09-16) are a separate layer. The address `(slot 20, password)` is what LCM tracks. Which device credential index holds it is decided by the provider, or by allocation, at write time.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

options.label: A: key by (slot, type) (Recommended)
options.description: One worker per lock keeps owning every exchange; Slot stays single-valued; re-key worker/registry/adapter/LockPort to a credential address.

options.label: B: worker per (lock, type)
options.description: Least core change, but duplicates per-lock pacing/offline/turn() across workers on the same radio.

options.label: C: slot holds a bundle
options.description: Keys unchanged; wrote/seen/repairs become per-type maps inside one Slot; partial sync within a slot.

content.text:
Here's what I found about the device index, which you decided on 2026-09-16 ("each credential type gets its own index on the lock, chosen when first set").

- On native-user locks (Z-Wave User Credential CC, Matter), LCM **finds its credentials through the tagged lock user** (`lcm:<slot>:`), not through the index (`_base.py:1273-1330`). The lock user is a persistent anchor: clearing a PIN leaves the user in place, and releasing a slot removes the user only "when it holds nothing else" (`_base.py:1768`).
- That makes your per-type index cheap for password. The Z-Wave provider can look up the tagged user's password credential wherever it sits. If there isn't one, it takes the lowest free password index. Matter already lets the lock pick the index (`credential_index_follows_slot = False`), so this follows an existing pattern. **Nothing needs to persist the index, and the sync core never sees it.** The address stays `(slot, password)`.
- PIN keeps following the slot on Z-Wave (`credential_index_follows_slot`), which your 09-16 note already leaned toward for back-compat.
- Release has to change in one place. Today it removes "its PIN, and the user itself only when it holds nothing else". It now has to remove the password LCM wrote as well. Otherwise a deleted user's password still opens the door, which is the #1453 bug again for a second type.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The user tag is what makes indexes free to move. Because LCM identifies its user by the tag and not by position, any credential type can sit at any index on that user. The tag rule from #1422 ("mutable values never go in identifiers") is what makes per-type indexes nearly free here.
- Virtual has no user records and keys by slot, so on Virtual the password index simply equals the slot. Only Z-Wave User Credential CC needs the allocation.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I have what I need for the first section. I'll present the design in parts and check each with you before moving on.

## Design, part 1 of 4: sync core and storage

**Credential address.** `CredentialAddress(slot, type)` already exists in `model/credentials.py`. It becomes the key throughout `sync/`:
- `LockWorker.slots: dict[CredentialAddress, Slot]`. `want`, `forget`, `status` and `push` take an address.
- `LockPort.read(addresses) -> {address: Reading}` and `LockPort.write(address, value)`.
- `sync/slot.py` keeps its single-value state machine. Only the names change: `Holds.pin` becomes `Holds.value` and `Want` becomes `str | None` for any type. `Holds.__repr__` keeps masking the value.
- Release stays per slot. When a slot leaves the entry, the worker releases every type it holds there in one provider call, so the provider can delete the lock user only after its last credential is gone.

**Which addresses a lock manages.** The managed addresses for a lock are the user's slot crossed with the intersection of `capabilities.credential_types` and `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, computed **per lock**. A lock without password never gets a password address, so it can't make the aggregate `in_sync` unavailable. This fixes the global `managed_addresses()` gap found in the #1572 review. `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` becomes `{PIN, PASSWORD}`. The available types for an entry are the union over its locks, and that union drives which entities and card tabs exist.

**Persistence (`ha/lock_store.py`, Store v1 → v2).** Each slot record becomes `{"wrote": {"pin": <fingerprint>, "password": REDACTED, "release": …}`. The migration moves an existing `wrote` under `"pin"`. The fingerprint also takes the type as input (`fingerprint(type, value, salt)`), so a PIN and a password with the same text don't produce the same fingerprint. No credential value is ever persisted, same as today.

**Config.** The user subentry gets an optional `password` alongside `pin`. Because it's optional and absent means "none", no config-entry migration is needed. The enable rule becomes "at least one credential of a type the entry offers". `pin_required` becomes `credential_required`, with a repair to match.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Keeping release at slot level while sync goes per address mirrors the lock itself. A lock user owns all of its credentials, and deleting the user deletes them all. If release went per address, the provider would have to work out when it was handling the last credential on the user.
- The Store migration is the only one-way step in this design. Everything else is additive, so if it ships as a minor release, a downgrade only fails to read v2 Store records. Downgrading is the case HA's `Store` versioning exists to refuse.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

content.text:
Agreed, and it matches your 09-16 note ("a user requires at least one supported credential"). On `main` the rule shows up in four places, and all four change to "no credential at all":

| Where | Today | After |
|---|---|---|
| `ha/slot_coordinator.py:294`, clearing a value | Clearing the PIN on an enabled slot sets `enabled: False` | Clearing any credential disables the slot only if **no other credential remains** |
| `ha/slot_coordinator.py:355`, enable toggle | Enabling without a PIN raises `PinRequiredError` and the `pin_required` repair | Refused only when the user has no credential of any type. Becomes `CredentialRequiredError` and the `credential_required` repair |
| `config_flow.py:84-93, 422`, setup and subentry forms | `_slot_enabled_without_pin` | `_slot_enabled_without_credential`, which checks every managed type's field |
| `switch.py:62`, `ha/services.py:451`, `repairs.py:179`, `__init__.py:1220` | Catch, route or clean up `pin_required_*` | Same for `credential_required_*`. Startup deletes any leftover `pin_required_*` issue so it doesn't linger after the upgrade |

There's one edge case I'll decide unless you object: a user whose only credential is a password, in an entry whose last password-capable lock was removed. Under the "keep the value, hide the entity" decision the password is still stored, so by your rule the user stays enabled. Each lock then correctly holds nothing for them, and their `in_sync` is on. I'll count any stored value, as you said, rather than "a value some lock can take".

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Counting stored values instead of currently-writable values keeps the enable state a pure function of the config. If it depended on lock capabilities, a lock dropping offline or getting re-interviewed could flip users between enabled and disabled. That's the coupling the condition → `allowed` gate work moved away from.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Design, part 2 of 4: providers

**Z-Wave (`providers/zwave_js.py`)**
- **Capabilities.** `async_get_capabilities` also reports `PASSWORD` from the same `supported_credential_types` read it already uses for PIN: slot count, min/max length, and `supports_learn`. A lock that doesn't advertise password is unchanged.
- **Read.** User records already carry password credentials. The PASSWORD type is already mapped (`zwave_js.py:163`). A read for `(slot, password)` finds the user tagged `lcm:<slot>:` and returns that user's password credential, wherever it sits, as `Holds`, `MASKED`, or `EMPTY`.
- **Write.** Look up the tagged user's password credential and overwrite it in place. If there isn't one, take the **lowest password index no user holds**, taken from the user list read just before the write. The user record is created on the first write of either type, the same way PIN works today.
- **Clear.** Delete only that password credential. The user stays as the anchor.
- **Release.** Remove every credential LCM wrote to the user (PIN and password), then remove the user only if it holds nothing else. A card or credential added in the vendor's app still protects the user from deletion.

**Virtual.** It already advertises every type. Its password is keyed by slot, like its PIN.

**Everything else** (Matter, ZHA, Z2M, Schlage, Akuvox, zwave-js-ui MQTT): no change. They don't advertise password, so the per-lock address rule from part 1 never gives them a password address.

**Base (`providers/_base.py`)**
- `_assert_slot_within_capacity` keeps checking the PIN count only, since password doesn't follow the slot.
- A password write on a lock with no free password index raises `LockOperationUnsupported`, naming the lock and its password slot count. The slot then holds with `CANT_SET`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- "Lowest index no user holds" has to come from the lock's user list, not from LCM's own records. A vendor-app credential at index 1 is invisible to LCM's store but very visible to the lock, and overwriting it would silently replace a code someone else added. This is the same "allocation refuses to write over a code it can still read" rule that `_base.py:1783` states for slots.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Does part 2 look right? One thing to check: when a lock is out of password indexes, I've made that a per-slot `CANT_SET` hold, the same as a PIN slot past capacity, not an entry-level error.

content.text:
The lock card is a different question from the slot card. The slot card shows one user. The lock card (`ts/lock-codes-card.ts`) shows **what one lock holds**: one chip per position on the lock, with ranges of empty positions collapsed ("Slots 4–10"), managed codes linked to their entry, and unmanaged codes editable through `write_unmanaged_code`. Its data is the worker's view of the lock (`websocket.py:644`, `lock_codes()`), keyed by slot.

Password breaks the card's main assumption, that a chip's number is a position on the lock:
- On Z-Wave, a PIN's lock index **is** the slot, so the PIN chips stay accurate.
- A password sits at an index LCM chose. The worker knows it as `(slot 20, password)`, and the index exists only inside the provider.
- In the first release, a password LCM doesn't manage (one added in the vendor's app) has no address at all, so the worker never sees it.

Three ways to handle it:

1. **Type tabs on the lock card** (recommended). The tabs match the slot card and appear only when the lock takes more than one managed type. The **PIN tab is exactly today's card.** The **Password tab** has one chip per user holding a password on this lock, labeled with the user's name and slot, the entry, sync state, and the masked value with reveal. It has no empty-position ranges, because LCM doesn't model password positions, and no unmanaged editing. Each type has its own capacity and length limits on the lock, so splitting by type matches how the lock itself is organized.
2. **Both credentials on each managed chip.** A managed user's chip gains a password line under the PIN. There are no tabs, but the chip's number now means "user" for one line and "position on the lock" for the other. A user who has only a password needs a chip with no PIN position, which the ranges and grouping logic (`_renderGroupsWithBorrowing`) wasn't built for.
3. **The lock card stays PIN-only for now.** Passwords appear only on the slot card, with a follow-up issue for the lock card. This is the least work, but a lock holding LCM passwords looks like it holds less than it does, which is exactly what this card exists to show.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Option 2's trouble comes from one integer meaning two things: the lock's index for a PIN, and LCM's slot for a password. Mixing those up is the "mutable values in identifiers" problem from #1422 again. Tabs avoid it because each tab has its own number space.
- Showing unmanaged passwords later doesn't need a new read. A Z-Wave User Credential read already returns every user with all of their credentials, vendor-app ones included. The Password tab can grow an "unmanaged" section later without the sync core knowing about it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Most of the per-type machinery already exists on `main`. Part 3 mostly connects password to it.

## Design, part 3 of 4: entities and validation

**Text entities (`text.py`)**
- Split `LockCodeManagerText` into `LockCodeManagerNameText` and a `LockCodeManagerCredentialText` base. The base holds `credential_type`, `TextMode.PASSWORD`, and a class-level `_attr_pattern`. `PinText` and `PasswordText` subclass it. `async_set_value` loses its `if self.key == CONF_PIN` branch and becomes `coordinator.async_request_credential_update(self.credential_type, value)`.
- **`PasswordText.pattern = r"^[\x20-\x7E]*$"`.** The `*` lets `""` through, so clearing still works.
- **`PinText` gets no pattern in this work.** HA re-checks `pattern` when it renders the state (`text/__init__.py:174`), so a stored PIN with a non-digit character would make the entity fail to render after the upgrade. A PIN pattern would need its own audit and migration, so it stays out of scope here.
- `native_min` and `native_max` stay permissive for both types, for the three reasons in `text.py:73-104`.
- Entities exist for **the types the entry offers** (the union across its locks). When a type stops being offered, its entity is removed and the stored value is kept (your 09-16 decision).

**One validator, every entry point.** A new `model/credentials.py` function, `validate_credential_value(type, value)`, checks the character set: digits for PIN, printable ASCII for password. The text entity's pattern, the config flow, `add_user` / `set_credential`, and the coordinator all call it, so YAML and services can't store a value the entity would then fail to render. **Passwords aren't stripped**, because a space is a legal character in one. PINs keep `vol.Strip`.

**Length, per lock.** `_validate_credential_length(value, type)` is already generic (`slot_coordinator.py:303`). It just gets called with `PASSWORD`, checking only the locks that take password. The error already names each lock and its range: "PASSWORD length 5 is not accepted by all locks: 8-32 characters for Front Door".

**Already per-type, so this is one line.** Add `"password": "Password"` to `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` (`const.py:210`, mirrored in `ts/const.ts`, which a contract test checks). That one line gives you:
- a `password_in_sync` sensor that's disabled by default (`binary_sensor.py:163`) while the aggregate `in_sync` stays enabled;
- password added to `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS`, so diagnostics redact it;
- `credential_used` events listing password once it's a managed type (`event.py:122`).

**Other rules**
- **Duplicates.** Setting a password another user in the entry already has is refused. The same text as someone's PIN is allowed.
- **Masking.** `Holds.__repr__` already masks the value. `mask_pin` becomes `mask_credential` and is used in every log line that carries a credential value.
- **Generator.** `generate_pin` becomes `generate_credential(type, length)`. For password it draws from the same printable-ASCII set and lands inside the length range of every password-capable lock in the entry.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The three uses of `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` are why the #1572 per-type sensor work paid off. The labels map was built as a single switch for "which types exist", and password is the first time it gets used for that.
- A pattern only constrains values going forward, but HA checks it when rendering values that are already stored. That's why the validator has to cover every way a value can get in (YAML, services, flows), not only the entity.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Does part 3 look right? Two choices to check: no pattern on PIN for now, and passwords not stripped.
Yes. Wondering if we should avoid the pattern on password too and just validate upstream

Agreed. Drop it. The deciding reason is something I didn't mention before: **HA's pattern error puts the value itself in the message.**

```python
# homeassistant/components/text/__init__.py:82-86
raise ValueError(
    f"Value {value} for {entity.entity_id}"
    f" doesn't match pattern {entity.pattern}"
)
```

A password with a tab or an emoji in it would show up in cleartext in the frontend toast and in any log that records the exception. The `native_min`/`native_max` checks have the same leak (lines 73-80), which is one more reason the PIN entity already avoids them.

Dropping it costs nothing. `text.set_value` ends in `entity.async_set_value`, which calls the coordinator, so `validate_credential_value` still checks every value. It also gives a better error: "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces", with no value echoed and no regex shown. It also removes the render-time failure, so the PIN and password entities end up following the same rule.

Updated part 3: **neither credential entity sets `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. The validator and the per-lock length check in the coordinator are the only gates, and their errors never include the value.**

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This is the third time HA's built-in `TextEntity` validation has been the wrong tool here: min blocks clearing, max cuts off typing silently, and pattern leaks the value. Each was reasonable on its own. Together they amount to a rule: in this integration, credential entities are thin pipes, and all validation lives in the coordinator.
- Holding to "errors never include the value" needs a test. A coordinator test can submit a value with a known marker (an invalid character plus a unique string) and assert the marker appears in neither the raised message nor `caplog`.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Design, part 4 of 4: config, services, cards, testing, PR order

**Config and services**
- The user subentry form gets an optional `password` field, shown only when one of the entry's locks takes password. Setup YAML gets `password:` per user.
- `add_user` gets `password`. `set_credential` and `clear_credential` already take `credential_type`. The `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` gate in `ha/services.py:186` opens on its own once password is in the set.
- Before release, check the blueprints and `services.yaml` for PIN-only assumptions. A shipped blueprint isn't type-checked, so this is a manual check.

**Websocket.** The card ships with the integration, so these payloads are internal and can change freely.
- `subscribe_code_slot` gains `credentials: {pin: {...}, password: REDACTED`, each with value-or-length, `in_sync` and state, plus `available_types`.
- `subscribe_lock_codes` keeps `slots` as the PIN view and adds `credentials.password`: one entry per managed user holding a password on this lock.

**Cards**
- **Slot card:** layout A. Tabs appear only when there's more than one type, and each tab's dot shows that type's sync state. Only the value field changes per tab. The edit input takes `inputmode` per type (`numeric` for PIN, `text` for password), and a length hint under it comes from the lock ranges.
- **Add-user card:** the same tabs on its credential input, and the generator works per type.
- **Lock card:** type tabs. The PIN tab is today's card, and the Password tab lists users.

**Testing.** I'll follow your order: property, then end-to-end, then integration, then unit.
- **Property:** the Hypothesis stateful sync property runs over `(slot, type)` addresses with both types. The invariants: each type converges independently, a lock without password never gets a password address, and release leaves no LCM credential behind on the lock.
- **End-to-end:** Virtual, which advertises every type, plus Z-Wave. The Z-Wave fixture is **a real node dump of a User Credential CC lock that advertises password**, cited by source and not hand-built. If none exists, I'll stop and ask rather than make one up.
- **Mutation checks:** the per-lock address filter, release removing the password, the "lowest index no user holds" rule, and "a clear disables only when no credential remains".

**PR order.** These all land on a branch, and the minor release ships after PR 4.
1. **Re-key the core to `CredentialAddress`, plus the Store v2 migration.** No behavior change, since every address is still PIN. That makes the existing suite a strict oracle: any test failure is a bug.
2. **Turn on password in the model and the HA layer.** `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, per-lock addresses, the credential-required rule, the validator, the text entity split, config and services, `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`. Exercised end to end on Virtual.
3. **Z-Wave provider.** Capabilities, read, allocation on write, clear, and release.
4. **Cards.** Slot card, add-user card, lock card.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- PR 1 doing nothing visible is deliberate. It's sub-project A's "re-key with no behavior change" from the 08-16 spec, and it's the cheapest point to catch a re-keying mistake: the suite and properties are an exact oracle there, and they stop being one once PR 2 changes behavior.
- Putting Virtual before Z-Wave means PR 2 tests the type plumbing with a provider that can't misbehave. When PR 3 fails, the cause is the Z-Wave index allocation, not the core.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Does part 4 look right? If it does, I'll write the spec to `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md`. It stays local and uncommitted, since `docs/` is gitignored and your specs rule says to write specs but never commit them. Then I'll ask you to review it before the implementation plan.

# Password credentials

**Date:** 2026-10-22. **Status:** design approved in conversation; spec awaiting review.
**Base:** `origin/main` at `ce1e1088` (clean-room core merged in #1702).
**Builds on:** `2026-08-16-user-centric-credential-model-design.md` (sub-project C, never specced until now) and the 2026-09-16 multi-credential decisions (memory `project_multi_credential_types_plan`).

## Goal

A user can hold a password as well as, or instead of, a PIN. Lock Code Manager writes it to every lock in the entry that takes passwords and keeps it in sync there, the way it does PINs today.

## Scope

In:

- Password as a second managed credential type, end to end: sync core, storage, Z-Wave and Virtual providers, entities, config, services, websocket, slot card, add-user card and lock card.
- Making the core type-generic, so that RFID and NFC can later be added as data, not as structure.

Out:

- RFID, NFC and biometrics.
- A pattern on the PIN entity (see "Text entities").
- Showing or editing unmanaged passwords on the lock card.
- User Code CC locks whose keypad accepts non-digit characters. The driver uses the Password type for these (`node-zwave-js AccessControl.ts:1598`), and they may be invisible to Lock Code Manager today. Follow-up issue.

## Decisions

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| 1 | Passwords are printable ASCII, 0x20–0x7E, spaces included. One character is one byte, so a lock's length limits mean what the user sees. On the wire, Z-Wave's credential length is a byte count (`UserCredentialCC.ts:2716`), and the driver decodes passwords as UTF-8 (`:82`). |
| 2 | The sync core is keyed by `CredentialAddress(slot, type)`. There is still one worker per lock. |
| 3 | Release stays per slot: one release removes every type Lock Code Manager wrote for the slot. |
| 4 | A slot needs at least one credential of any type. Clearing a credential disables the slot only when no other credential remains. A stored value counts even if no current lock takes its type. |
| 5 | On Z-Wave, the password index is allocated by the provider: it finds the tagged user's password wherever it is, or else takes the lowest password index no user holds. PIN keeps following the slot. |
| 6 | Credential text entities set no `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. One validator and the coordinator's per-lock length check are the only gates, and their errors never contain the value. |
| 7 | Passwords are not whitespace-stripped. PINs keep `vol.Strip`. |
| 8 | Slot card: tabs per type over one value field, each tab's dot showing that type's sync state. Tabs appear only when the entry offers more than one type. |
| 9 | Lock card: tabs per type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab lists managed users' passwords on that lock. |
| 10 | Carried from 2026-09-16: an entry's available types are the union across its locks. A type no longer offered keeps its stored value, and its entity is removed. Per-type in-sync sensors are disabled by default. Duplicates are refused within a type and allowed across types. The generator covers passwords. |

## Sync core

`CredentialAddress(user_ref, credential_type)` already exists (`model/credentials.py`). It becomes the key everywhere in `sync/`:

- `LockWorker.slots: dict[CredentialAddress, Slot]`. `want`, `forget`, `resume`, `status`, `syncing` and `push` take an address.
- `LockPort.read(addresses) -> Mapping[CredentialAddress, Reading]` and `LockPort.write(address, value) -> bool | None`.
- `sync/slot.py` stays a single-value state machine. `Holds.pin` becomes `Holds.value`, `Want` stays `str | None`, and `Holds.__repr__` keeps masking.
- `sync/registry.py` and `ha/adapter.py` re-key to match. The adapter turns an address into the provider call for that type.
- Release is per slot. When a slot leaves the entry, the worker sends one release for the slot. The provider removes every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to that slot's user, then the user only if it holds nothing else.

**Managed addresses are per lock:** `{CredentialAddress(slot, t) for t in user_types ∩ lock.capabilities.credential_types ∩ MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES}`. A lock that doesn't take password never gets a password address, so the aggregate `in_sync` on that lock ignores the type. This fixes the global `managed_addresses()` gap found in the #1572 review. Recompute when a lock is added or removed and when capabilities refresh.

`MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` becomes `{PIN, PASSWORD}`.

## Storage

`ha/lock_store.py`, `STORE_VERSION` 1 → 2.

- v1 slot record: `{"wrote": <fingerprint|cleared>, …release fields}`.
- v2 slot record: `{"wrote": {"pin": <fingerprint|cleared>, "password": REDACTED, …release fields}`.
- Migration: move v1 `wrote` under `"pin"`. Release fields stay at slot level.
- The fingerprint covers the type: `fingerprint(type, value, salt)`. Credential values are never persisted.

The Store migration is the only one-way step. Downgrading leaves a v2 Store the old version can't read, and HA's Store versioning is there to refuse that.

## Configuration and the credential-required rule

- The user subentry gets an optional `password` (absent means none), and setup YAML gets `password:` per user. No config-entry migration is needed.
- The rule changes in four places:
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:294`: clearing any credential disables an enabled slot only if no other credential remains.
  - `ha/slot_coordinator.py:355`: enabling is refused only when the user has no credential of any type. `PinRequiredError` becomes `CredentialRequiredError`.
  - `config_flow.py:84-93, 422`: `_slot_enabled_without_pin` becomes `_slot_enabled_without_credential`, which checks every managed type's field.
  - Repair `pin_required` becomes `credential_required`. Update `switch.py:62`, `ha/services.py:451`, `repairs.py:179` and `__init__.py:1220`. At startup, delete any leftover `pin_required_*` issue.

## Providers

**Z-Wave (`providers/zwave_js.py`)**

- **Capabilities:** also report `PASSWORD` from the same `supported_credential_types` read: slot count, min/max length and `supports_learn`. A lock without password is unchanged.
- **Read `(slot, password)`:** find the user tagged `lcm:<slot>:` and return its password credential, wherever it sits, as `Holds`, `MASKED` or `EMPTY`.
- **Write:** overwrite the tagged user's password credential in place. If it has none, use the lowest password index **no user on the lock holds**, taken from the user list read just before the write, so vendor-app credentials are never overwritten. Create the user on the first write of either type, as PIN does now.
- **Clear:** delete that password credential only. The user stays.
- **Release:** delete every credential Lock Code Manager wrote to the user (PIN and password), then the user only if it holds nothing else.
- **No free index:** raise `LockOperationUnsupported`, naming the lock and its password slot count. The address holds as `CANT_SET`.

**Virtual:** already advertises every type. Its password is keyed by slot.

**Base (`providers/_base.py`):** `_assert_slot_within_capacity` stays PIN-only, because password doesn't follow the slot.

**Everyone else** (Matter, ZHA, Z2M, Schlage, Akuvox, zwave-js-ui MQTT): no change. None of them advertises password.

## Entities and validation

**Text entities (`text.py`)**

- Split `LockCodeManagerText` into `LockCodeManagerNameText` and `LockCodeManagerCredentialText(credential_type)`, with subclasses `PinText` and `PasswordText`. All credential entities use `TextMode.PASSWORD`.
- `async_set_value` calls `coordinator.async_request_credential_update(type, value)`.
- No `pattern`, `native_min` or `native_max`. HA's own errors embed the cleartext value (`homeassistant/components/text/__init__.py:73-86`), and it re-checks them when rendering state (`:162-178`).
- Credential entities exist for the entry's available types. They're added and removed as that union changes.

**Validator:** `model/credentials.py: validate_credential_value(type, value)` checks the character set: digits for PIN, 0x20–0x7E for password. It's called from the coordinator, the config flow, `add_user`, `set_credential` and the setup YAML schema. Error text names the rule and never the value. For example: "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces".

**Length:** `_validate_credential_length(value, type)` (`slot_coordinator.py:303`) is called for password against password-capable locks only. Its message already names each lock and its range.

**Labels:** add `"password": "Password"` to `CREDENTIAL_LABELS` (`const.py:210`) and `ts/const.ts`, which a contract test checks. That gives:
- the `password_in_sync` sensor, disabled by default (`binary_sensor.py:163`);
- password in `SENSITIVE_ENTITY_KEYS`, so diagnostics redact it;
- password in the event entity's types (`event.py:122`).

**Duplicates:** refuse a password another user in the entry already holds.

**Masking:** `mask_pin` becomes `mask_credential`, used in every log line that carries a value.

**Generator:** `generate_pin` becomes `generate_credential(type, length)`. For password it uses the printable ASCII set, at a length inside every password-capable lock's range in the entry.

## Services and websocket

- `add_user` gets `password`. `set_credential` and `clear_credential` accept `password` once it's in `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES` (`ha/services.py:186`).
- `subscribe_code_slot` gets `available_types` and `credentials: {<type>: {value | length, in_sync, state}}`.
- `subscribe_lock_codes` keeps `slots` as the PIN view and adds `credentials.password`: one entry per managed user holding a password on this lock (slot, name, entry, value or length, in_sync).
- These payloads are internal. The card ships with the integration.
- Before release, check blueprints and `services.yaml` for PIN-only assumptions.

## Cards

- **Slot card (`ts/slot-card.ts`):**
  - The type tabs sit between the name and the value row. Each tab's dot shows that type's sync state: in sync, or pending or held.
  - Only the value field changes per tab. The name, enable switch, conditions and lock list stay the same.
  - The edit input sets `inputmode` per type (today it's hard-coded `numeric` at `:607`) and shows a length hint from the lock ranges.
  - With one available type, the card renders exactly as it does today.
- **Add-user card (`ts/add-user-card.ts`):** the same tabs on the credential input, with a per-type generator.
- **Lock card (`ts/lock-codes-card.ts`):** the type tabs appear when the lock takes more than one managed type. The PIN tab is today's card. The Password tab has one chip per managed user, with no empty-position ranges and no unmanaged editing.

## Testing

Order: property, then end-to-end, then integration, then unit.

- **Property:** the Hypothesis stateful sync property runs over `(slot, type)` addresses with both types. Invariants:
  - each type converges independently;
  - a lock without password never gets a password address;
  - after release, no Lock Code Manager credential remains on the lock.
- **End-to-end:** Virtual for all types. Z-Wave uses a **sourced** node dump of a User Credential CC lock that advertises password, cited by source. If none exists, stop and ask rather than make one up.
- **Leak test:** submit an invalid value carrying a unique marker. Assert the marker appears in neither the raised error nor `caplog`.
- **Mutation checks:** the per-lock address filter, release removing the password, the "lowest index no user holds" rule, and "a clear disables only when no credential remains".

## PR order

Each PR is reviewed on its own. The minor release ships after PR 4.

1. **Core re-key to `CredentialAddress`, plus Store v2.** No behavior change, since every address is PIN, so the existing suite and properties are a strict oracle.
2. **Password in the model and HA layer:** `MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES`, per-lock addresses, the credential-required rule, the validator, the text entity split, config and services, `CREDENTIAL_LABELS`. Exercised on Virtual.
3. **Z-Wave provider:** capabilities, read, allocation on write, clear, release.
4. **Cards:** slot card, add-user card, lock card.

## Open items

- The sourced Z-Wave User Credential CC dump with password capability (blocks PR 3 tests).
- The follow-up issue for User Code CC alphanumeric locks.
